headline: The 5:52 ebb: bass stacked on the East End rip, bluefish crashing through, bonito on the doorstep
subhead: Four days out from the new moon, the Canal's current is loading up and the bite is sharpening right on schedule.
body_markdown:
5:52 this morning, East End, and the current was already running better than three and a half knots off the Bourne bridge rip. That's early for this kind of push — we're not even at the new moon yet, four days out from the 12th, and the Canal's already tightening its belt. I stood on the rocks below the Railroad Bridge and watched the rip stand up hard against the light east breeze, and inside of twenty minutes I had two bass in the 28-30 inch range come off a white Savage Gear sand eel, fished on the swing and let it stall right where the seam folds back on itself.

We flagged this last week — said building tidal flow into the new moon should sharpen the bite at current-driven structure, and that's exactly what's playing out. The Canal doesn't care what the calendar says about summer doldrums. It cares about how much water is moving, and right now there's more water moving through that ditch than there's been in three weeks. Every stage of the tide is running harder, which means the transition windows — the hour before and after max ebb or max flood — are producing more consistent hits instead of the stop-and-start pecking we had through late July.

East End remains the show for bass. The rip off the Bourne side, especially on the back half of the ebb when the current's still hauling but starting to organize into a cleaner standing wave, is where the fish are holding tightest. Eels — live ones if you can get them, otherwise the soft-plastic imitations — worked on a slow drop-back through the foam line have been the most consistent producer. Bucktails in the 1.5 to 2-ounce range, white or olive, dragged bottom on the last hour of ebb before the slack, have also been picking off fish that are sitting deeper in the trough. Bluefish are mixed in and aggressive, mostly in the 3 to 6 pound class, and they'll murder a topwater plug worked through the rip on the last of the flood before the water goes flat. If you're throwing metal for bass and keep getting your leader shredded, that's your bluefish answer right there — don't fight it, just switch over for twenty minutes and have some fun with them.

West End is a different animal right now, and it's worth paying attention to why. Mashnee Island and the seam off Hog Island have been holding a scattered but real fluke bite — nothing to write home about, three or four keepers in a good session on Gulp swimming mullets bounced along the bottom on the last of the incoming, but enough to make the drift worthwhile if bass aren't cooperating. The real story at the west end this week is what's not here yet but is close. Buzzards Bay is seeing the first real bonito push cross over from the Rhode Island side, and Phinneys Harbor and the water off Wings Neck are exactly the kind of current-seam structure that lights up when those fish decide to run the Canal's mouth chasing bait. I haven't had a confirmed bonito in hand yet out of the west end this week, and I'm not going to tell you they're stacked up because they're not — but the conditions are lining up. Building tidal flow, warming inshore water, bait getting pushed hard through the seams — that's the recipe, and it's the same recipe that's already put bonito into the Watch Hill-to-Sakonnet corridor and pushed them into the Bay itself. If I had one morning to gamble on it this week, I'd fish the last two hours of the ebb off Mashnee with a small metal — a half-ounce Deadly Dick or similar — and I'd be ready to change my whole game plan if I saw fish busting bait on the surface.

Slack water, both ends, has been mostly dead the last ten days, and that hasn't changed. If you're canal fishing and you show up at true slack expecting action, you're going to stand there with a rod in your hand and nothing on the end of it. That's always been the rule here — the fish feed on current, not on stillness — but with the tidal range building toward the new moon, the dead slack windows are getting shorter and the transition into moving water is getting sharper. That's good news if you're the kind of angler who can read a tide chart and show up twenty minutes before the turn instead of twenty minutes after.

Looking at the next several days, I expect this pattern to keep sharpening right into the 12th. Bigger tidal range means faster current, faster current means the rips stand up harder and hold bait tighter, and that should mean more consistent bass and bluefish action at both ends through the weekend. Scusset side has had a quieter week for me — some short bass mixed with schoolie bluefish on small metal in the surf off the beach, nothing worth planning a trip around specifically, but worth a stop if you're already out there working the east end and want to check the surf on your way in. The bonito watch is the thing I'll be paying closest attention to over the next 72 hours — if that Buzzards Bay push keeps advancing the way it's been advancing, the west end could get interesting fast, and I'd rather be standing there with a bag of small metal in hand when it happens than reading about it after the fact.
